transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Carva Coleman.
Forecasters say Hurricane Isaias has become a major Category 3 storm, with top sustained
winds of 120 miles per hour.
Isaias is now 170 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi, expected to make landfall
late tonight.
The winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize is former UN Human Rights Chief Navi Pillay.
As Esme Nicholson reports, the prize committee honored her efforts to promote peace via international
law.
Navi Pillay, who reacted with disbelief when she heard the news this morning, started her
career defending Nelson Mandela.
After apartheid, she became a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda,
where she helped establish groundbreaking legal precedents recognizing rape as an act
of genocide.
She chaired the UN International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory
that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.
Israel has dismissed the report as scandalous.
And today, 85-year-old Pillay is serving as a judge at the International Court of Justice
in a case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide.
Chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, Jürgen Vatner Friedness, praised her firm moral compass
and work that shows legal measures can prevent acts of war.
For NPR News, I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin.
The Ukrainian military is using novel methods to push Russian troops out of the eastern
Ukrainian region of Donbas.
NPR's Joanna Kekissis reports on how the Ukrainians have reclaimed more territory from the Russians.
The military says its soldiers used electronic warfare and aerial drones to blind Russian
reconnaissance.
And then they destroyed Russian firepower and supply routes.
And then after that, they sent in land robots, which are these unmanned ground vehicles that
look like small trucks, to weaken Russian positions.
And then assault groups went in to clear those positions.
The Ukrainians say they took back roughly 68 square miles, and that's about three times
the size of Manhattan.
And Pierre's Joanna Kekissis reporting.
Russia's been firing drones and missiles at civilian targets in Ukraine this week.
Ukrainian officials say at least 85 people have been killed.
Mortgage rates are up again.
The national average for a 30-year fixed rate is now 7.4 percent.
Pierre Stephen Bisaha reports.
It wasn't that long ago, back in February, when mortgage rates had fallen below 6 percent.
But since then, two major events have caused a sharp jump in the cost of borrowing, including
for a house.
The first was the start of the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran.
That caused investors to worry about inflation, which caused bond yields to rise.
The second event was the Federal Reserve raising interest rates last month to fight that inflation.
Markets quickly climbed past 7 percent, and they've kept climbing since.
The Fed will meet later this month to decide on whether to again hike rates, which could
drive mortgage rates up even higher.
Stephen Bisaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
This is NPR.
The federal deficit was nearly $2 trillion for the just-ended fiscal year.
Tax revenues were up, but NPR's Scott Horsley reports government spending grew even faster.
According to the Congressional Budget Office, the 2026 federal deficit is more than $200
billion bigger than last year's, a staggering level of red ink for a country that's not
in recession or a widespread war.
The government collected more money from income and payroll taxes during the year, while corporate
tax receipts were somewhat lower.
The increased revenue was more than offset, though, by higher spending on programs like
Social Security and Medicare.
The government also spent well over a trillion dollars during the year just to cover interest
payments on the debt.
Those interest payments have been climbing as a result of the government's mounting pile
of IOUs and rising interest rates.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
The NFL has joined New Jersey in asking the U.S. Supreme Court to let states regulate
sports betting.
The case stems from a dispute over prediction markets such as Kalshi.
The pro-football league argues this is gambling.
Kalshi argues these exchanges are financial swaps, and only the federal government should
regulate them.
The U.S. Army has found several rather systematic errors contributed to a deadly crash near
Reagan National Airport in 2025.
Sixty-seven people were killed when a passenger jet collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter.
The Army report noted failures with procedure and communication.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News.
This message comes from NPR sponsor Charles Schwab.
Is there a right time to sell a stock?
Are you taking the right risks with your portfolio?
Financial decisions can be tricky, and often your own cognitive and emotional biases can
lead you astray.
Financial decoder, an original podcast from Charles Schwab, can help.
Join host Mark Reapie as he offers practical solutions to help overcome the biases that
may affect your investing decisions.
Download the latest episode and subscribe at Schwab.com/financialdecoder.

topics.text: Hurricane Isaias strengthens to Category 3 storm, 170 miles south of Mississippi River mouth
Navi Pillay, former UN Human Rights Chief, wins 2024 Nobel Peace Prize
Ukrainian military uses drones and robots to reclaim 68 square miles from Russians in Donbas
Russia fires drones and missiles at Ukrainian civilian targets, killing at least 85 people
Mortgage rates rise to 7.4 percent for 30-year fixed loans amid inflation concerns
Federal deficit reaches nearly $2 trillion for fiscal year 2026, highest in non-crisis period
NFL joins New Jersey asking Supreme Court to let states regulate sports betting markets
Army investigation finds systematic errors contributed to Reagan National Airport plane-helicopter collision killing 67
